chapter_theme: Sivavakkiyar turns from the yogic body (breath, the letters a and u, the nine gates, the middle channel) to a running attack on the rules of pollution, on caste, on book-knowledge and on worship of worn or built lingas, arguing each time from the body itself: the body that was formed from menstrual blood and semen, that holds the Lord within, and that ends deeds by the breath. The chapter closes with a short run of first-person verses on the oneness of 'you and I'.
structure_note: 1414 to 1419 are chained by their opening words (ஆனதே, உலாவும், கும்பிடும், நீங்கும்) and describe the yogic state; 1420 to 1424 are questions put to jnanis and ritualists; 1425 to 1427 attack caste; 1428 to 1432 attack external worship; 1433 and 1434 are personal; 1435 to 1438 return to the attack on penance and books.

1414.reading: There is nothing else: breath, substance and body are the state given where the good Lord's feet join; when love in me endures and I work the breath, the old deeds say 'leave' and go far, far away.
1414.nuance: வாசியை வருந்தினால் is the verse's hinge: வாசி is the Siddhars' word for the breath worked as a practice, and வருந்துதல் (to labour, press) takes it as effort on the breath. The first two lines are compressed and their syntax is loose; the plain sense is that deeds depart when breath practice and love go together.

1415.reading: Pati has come to be; pasu and pasam have ceased; the malas, the senses and the deeds are gone. Did wind come and meet a fire set in the forest? Within the flesh, fixing on the air, one roams in union with it.
1415.nuance: The three terms of Saiva Siddhanta, pati, pasu and pasam, open the verse, and the fire-in-the-forest question is a figure for how quickly bonds burn when the breath (வாயு) is joined to them. The chained opening (ஆனதே from 1414's last word) marks this run of verses as one sequence.

1416.reading: What rose and pressed in as 'u' and 'a' roams; the five senses that roamed rest in one place; the moon there becomes love, stands, and nectar is eaten; mark and know our Lord who roams, and worship him.
1416.nuance: உவ்வும் அவ்வும் are the letters உ and அ of the pranava, and in the Siddhars' usage also the two breaths or the two channels; the moon that becomes love and yields nectar is, as tradition takes it, the inner moon at the crown. A plain reading has the senses stilled and a sweetness tasted; the coded one maps each term to a body-place.

1417.reading: Within the worshipping thought, trusting Guhan and the five-handed one, seeking them at left and right as ours; seating our Lord and the Mother and the one in the middle; as a bee follows, the word follows on, and sloth departs.
1417.nuance: Murugan (குகன்) and Ganesha (ஐங்கரன்) at left and right, with the Lord and the Mother and a middle one (நடுவன்), reads in tradition as the three channels: the left and right nadis and the central one. The plain reading is a devotional placement of the family of Siva. தும்பிபோல வாசகம் (the word like a bee) may be the hum of the mantra.

1418.reading: The five senses depart, and the heaped strong deeds, and the desire that is ego; from within the Omkara, when the nine have ceased and one stands in the one, to stand resolved by the word of the sleepless Lord is purity.
1418.nuance: ஒன்பதொழிந்து ஒன்றில் (nine ceased, in the one) is usually taken as the nine gates of the body closed and attention held in the one opening above, as in 1452; it could also count nine of something else. அருந்தடந்த பாதமும் is hard to construe. Purity (சுத்தம்) here is defined by this inner standing, which sets up the attacks on ritual purity that follow.

1419.reading: From the time I was mingled in the womb, the cause I saw standing: was it not when form mingled with form that I knew you? Whatever I give up, whatever I hide, in every time I assented to deeds, when we stood mingled in form, were you and I not one?
1419.nuance: A first-person verse of non-duality: the speaker says the Lord and he have been one since conception, through every deed. விரக்கில் என் மறைக்கில் என் is loose; I take it as 'whether I renounce or conceal'. The closing question (ஒன்றலோ) is rhetorical.

1420.reading: Yogis who hunted out the books of knowledge and recited them: you have not sought and known within the light that is knowledge; once the Lord who stands as knowledge is known, there is nothing other than knowledge, and what we have said is true.
1420.nuance: ஞானம் is used four times, moving from a thing in books to the Lord himself: the argument is that knowledge is not about the Lord but is the Lord, so reading about it misses it.

1421.reading: Before conception, where did the body stand? Before it took form, where did the breath of life stand? In the thought wrapped in confusion, where did delusion stand? Jnanis who have come to know what you desired, you must explain this at length.
1421.nuance: Three questions on origins, each ending எவ்விடம் (where), put as a challenge to professed jnanis. The verse does not answer them; whether it means the answers are unknowable or that they are the test of real knowledge is left open.

1422.reading: The seven kinds of birth taken as seed within the womb whirl, born and dying, by the fruit of the two deeds; once the three times of further births by further deeds are apportioned, the jnani who knows says, 'this is the fruit of deed that falls due.'
1422.nuance: ஏழு தோற்றம் is the conventional seven classes of birth; இருவினை the good and bad deeds; மூன்று காலம் the three times. The verse is a compact statement of karma, and the last line may mean that only the jnani can read a present state as the fruit of a deed.

1423.reading: You drink water and spit so that the spittle leaves the mouth; while the mouth remains, where has the spittle gone? Is not the mantra you utter the spittle of that mouth? And when the dog is known, what spittle is there left to seek?
1423.nuance: The attack on எச்சில் (saliva as pollution) turns the rule against the ritualist: the mantra comes from the same wet mouth. The last line is obscure; நாயினை அறிந்தபோது may mean 'once you know the dog', the animal whose saliva is the type of pollution, or may be self-abasing ('this dog, myself').

1424.reading: Dumb ones who start to fall into water saying 'it is pollution': where was the pollution, and where was the purifying? If you could know how pollution arose and make yourselves pure, you could follow and see the light that has no pollution.
1424.nuance: தொடக்கு means both ritual pollution and beginning, so தொடக்கிலாத சோதி is at once the light without pollution and the light without beginning; the pun carries the argument that true purity is knowing the origin of impurity, not washing.

1425.reading: If a buffalo and a cow mated in desire, the form born would show the difference of kind, as is the way; but when a reciter of the Veda goes and joins an outcaste woman, tell me how it is that the child is born with no such difference.
1425.nuance: The argument is from breeding: species differences show in the offspring, caste differences do not, so caste is not in the body. புலைச்சி (woman of the puaiya caste) and வேதம் ஓதுவான் are the two poles of the hierarchy, chosen for the sharpest case.

1426.reading: People who talk of kinds of clans and argue the cases: once you seek and understand the straight truth of all these clans summed up, you find nothing there but a surplus of semen; and daily you seek to burn Manu, to be laughed at.
1426.nuance: சுக்கிலம் (semen) is the whole material basis the verse allows to lineage. The last line is unclear: மனு எரிக்க may be 'to kindle (recite) Manu', the law-book of caste, or 'to burn' it; either way the clan-talkers are made laughable.

1427.reading: The four Vedas recited, the shastras they expounded, the tattvas of the elements, the Agamas that fit them, the 'truth' of caste difference and the wavering books: all of it, born as difference upon difference, has whirled about and stayed.
1427.nuance: The verse lumps scripture and caste together as one product of division (பேதம்). It does not say the texts are false, only that they are born of and breed difference; that is a weaker and more precise charge than outright rejection.

1428.reading: Wearing the linga on your body you perform the puja of the whole universe; you whose chest has settled into wearing the body-linga, you run everywhere, lose your worth and perish: fools who look on brick, copper and stone as the best.
1428.nuance: அங்கலிங்கம் is the linga worn on the body, as Lingayats and some Saivas wear it; அகண்டபூசை may be the claim to worship the undivided whole through it. The materials of line 4 are the materials of built lingas, and the verse's charge is that worship has been fixed on substance.

1429.reading: Fools who bathe every day saying 'pollution, pollution': was it not as pollution that the body gathered and came to be? You ghouls who praise the locked body within you: when the pollution came and took hold, it was then that Sivaayam became clear.
1429.nuance: தீட்டம் is menstrual pollution, and the verse says the body itself was formed from it. The last line is hard: it may say that conception, the moment pollution 'took hold', is where Siva's work shows, or that pollution clears when its nature is understood. பூட்டகாயம் (locked body) is also unclear.

1430.reading: Above the navel, the four and the three are Om Namasivaya; you ghouls who proclaim 'sandhi, sandhi': coming first within us and going through the root channel, know and see the place where dusk and dawn have ceased.
1430.nuance: நாலுமூன்று (four and three) is unexplained; it may count the letters of ஓம் நமசிவாய as seven, or name body-places. சந்தி is the twilight rite; the verse opposes it to the inner place where there is no dusk or dawn, reached through the மூலநாடி. The sense turns on this cipher.

1431.reading: Our Lord who lives in the fire of the three fires: where did he fall in love while the virgin was within? Four heads, two hands, one of the two in the mind: think and think, drive it within yourselves, know and see.
1431.nuance: A cipher verse. கன்னி (the virgin) is read by tradition as the coiled Shakti at the root; the three fires and the four-headed one (Brahma) may name centres in the body. Nothing in the verse fixes these; the plain instruction is only to turn the question inward.

1432.reading: You too, doing service, run about in circles and die; having eaten and whirled about you never look intently within yourselves; our Lord who lives in groves where bees roam stands apart within you, as he did of old, the Lord himself.
1432.nuance: தொண்டு (service) is the servant's path of temple work, and the verse sets it among the things that wear a man out. பகுத்திருப்பன் (he stands distinguished, set apart) may mean the Lord sits within as a distinct presence, or that he has apportioned himself within each.

1433.reading: Supreme One, for you and me there is no other fear, see; to fold my hands to you daily is my duty; Lord of fame who melted the crown and gave nectar; the strength you gave me is truth, truth, truth.
1433.nuance: சிரமுருக்கி அமுதளித்த (melted the head and gave nectar) is, as tradition reads it, the nectar released at the crown in yoga; the verse itself is a plain address of trust. The folded hands of line 2 sit oddly beside the chapter's attacks on ritual, and show that the attack is on empty form, not on worship.

1434.reading: Within myself I ran everywhere seeking myself; within myself I found nothing but myself; as lightning that flashes in the sky subsides into the sky, within me there is nothing other than the Lord and I.
1434.nuance: The lightning image says the self appears and subsides in the same ground, which is the Lord. ஈசனோடு யானும் அல்லது இல்லை keeps two names, Lord and I, while denying anything else; whether that is two or one is left to the reader.

1435.reading: Preparing places, purifying, on the seat you have set up, smearing ash all over, you do rare penances; where does the knowledge of the Lord who withdraws arise? Where does it subside? Know that, and then do puja.
1435.nuance: The verse does not forbid puja; its last words are அறிந்து பூசை செய்யுமே, do puja knowing. ஒடுங்குகின்ற நாதனார் (the Lord who withdraws or contracts) may describe the Lord as he who draws all in, or as hidden.

1436.reading: Carrying books, you babble lies; you do not know how the place of dying and the place of being born are; if you could know and look at all that thought, the light within the Highest would become the enjoyment you know.
1436.nuance: புத்தகங்களைச் சுமந்து (carrying books) pictures learning as a load. The test the verse sets is knowledge of where one dies and is born, which it treats as inner knowledge, not book knowledge.

1437.reading: Born in grace and standing, you take the form of maya and waver in darkness, poor people, listen: if you can wear penance in the Substance and look fittingly, what delusion is there? Sivaayam is hidden in the fire.
1437.nuance: The verse says people are born in grace and only then take maya's form, which is a hopeful ordering. வன்னியின் மறைந்ததே சிவாயமே is the cipher: fire may be the body's fire, the fire of yoga, or the fire of tapas in which the five letters lie hidden.

1438.reading: Dregs whose thought has perished, whirling in the sun of karma-thought for as long as there is dharma-thought, without knowing tapas: the wealthy Lord who cannot be made clear though sought birth after birth, you must see with delight within yourselves, for your good.
1438.nuance: தன்மசிந்தை and கன்மசிந்தை (thought of dharma, thought of karma) are set as a pair and both treated as whirling; the verse seems to say that calculating merit is itself bondage. The first two lines are hard to parse and the reading is tentative.

links.note: Both make learning worthless without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning has gained if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge, and Sivavakkiyar tells the book-reciting yogis that there is no knowledge other than the Lord who stands as knowledge.

Tirumular says no purification is needed for one who stands free of தொடக்கு, and Sivavakkiyar says those who fall into water over தொடக்கு should instead learn where pollution arose; both move purity from the rite to the inner state, and both use the same word.

The Kural's many who bathe like the distinguished with impurity in their minds are Sivavakkiyar's 'dumb ones' who fall into water over pollution; the Kural's point is hypocrisy, Sivavakkiyar's that bathing cannot reach where impurity began.

The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from what they do; Sivavakkiyar argues the same from breeding: a Brahmin and an outcaste woman produce a child with no mark of difference, unlike a buffalo and a cow.

The Naladiyar calls 'good caste' and 'bad caste' mere words, made real only by tapas, learning and effort; Sivavakkiyar denies caste a basis in the body itself. The Jain text keeps a replacement standard, the Siddhar offers none.

Tirumular says that for those who have set Nandi in love there is no caste (குலமில்லை); Sivavakkiyar says that whoever looks into the clans finds nothing but semen. One removes caste at the end of the path, the other denies it at the root.

Tirumular lists copper, brick, bilva, gold and the rest and says any one of them, clearly known, can be the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar calls those who see excellence in brick, copper and stone fools. The conflict holds if Sivavakkiyar denies that any material can serve as the linga; it softens if his target is only those who stop at the material, since Tirumular also requires that it be 'clearly known'.

Tirumular has the devotee seek through lands, towns and temples and then find the Lord taking the joined heart as his temple; Sivavakkiyar says those who run about in service die of it and the Lord was within all along. Tirumular lets the outward road lead inward; Sivavakkiyar denies the road any part.

Tirumular saw the true substance within the body and came to cherish it as the Lord's temple; Sivavakkiyar searched within himself and found nothing other than the Lord and himself. Both locate the finding inside the body.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar tells those who prepare seats and smear ash to first know where knowledge of the Lord arises and subsides. Both put inner state before outward preparation, though the Kural's is moral and the Siddhar's is gnostic.

The Naladiyar separates those who collect books and fill the house from those who understand them; Sivavakkiyar's book-carriers babble lies and do not know where birth and death occur. Both make possessing books a different thing from knowing.

new_concepts.gloss: the breath worked as a practice; the Siddhars' word for breath control
new_concepts.label_source: Used in 1414 as வாசியை; also hidden in the mantra form சிவாயவசி of 1488

new_concepts.gloss: ritual pollution: menstrual pollution, saliva, birth and death pollution, and the rules of purification around them
new_concepts.label_source: Used in 1429 as தீட்டம், தீட்டு; 1423 and 1442 use எச்சில் and 1424 uses தொடக்கு for the same idea

source_issues: 1419 line 3 (விரக்கில்என் மறைக்கில்என்) is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
1426 line 4 (மனு எரிக்க) is unclear and may be a corrupt reading.
1429 line 3 (பூட்டகாயம்) is unclear; the word may be damaged.
